Appendix D. Agent-Based Simulations for Standard SAOMs

This section summarizes results from an agent-based computational experiment designed to evaluate the standard SAOM’s ability to capture an in silico data-generating process where depression-based tie creation and tie maintenance dynamics are distinct. In short, we employed an agent-based model (ABM) to simulate networks dependent upon a synthetic variable proxying adolescent depression (D). At baseline, we generate a random network with an outdegree distribution that reproduces the average outdegree of students in CILS4EU’s wave one data. Then, we simulate a chain of SAOM-like microsteps in which agents’ tie change decisions, namely, maintaining a current tie or creating a new tie, are governed by user-specified differences in agents’ tie creation and maintenance probabilities, which are in turn a function of agents’ (synthetic) depression variable, D.

ABM Pseudocode. The pseudocode below describes our ABM, that is, how we simulate the emergence of a random ‘wave two’ network based on agents’ D, where the baseline ‘wave one’ network is based on the average outdegree distribution observed in the CILS4EU dataset.

  1. Set the global parameters:
  1. N = 100, the number of agents.
  2. n = 30, the mean number of decisions to create or maintain ties per agent.
  3. Set nsteps=n⋅Nn_{steps} = n \cdot N , the total number of SAOM-like ‘microsteps.’
  4. Max degree_{degree} = 5, agents’ maximum possible outdegree (value taken from CILS4EU).
  5. Transition_Probability. This is the probability an agent i will choose to create a tie (vs. maintain a tie) when said agent has at least one outgoing tie but less than 5 outgoing ties. Transition_Probability values monotonically decrease as agents’ outdegree increases. This ensures the resulting ‘wave two’ network has a degree distribution similar to the observed in CILS4EU.
  6. Transition_Probability(change = creation| ∑jtieij=1\sum_{j} tie_{ij} = 1 ) = 0.7, probability an agent with outdegree = 1 will create a tie (v. maintain a tie).
  1. Transition_Probability(change = creation| ∑jtieij=2\sum_{j} tie_{ij} = 2 ) = 0.6, probability an agent with outdegree = 2 will create a tie (v. maintain a tie).
  2. Transition_Probability(change = creation| ∑jtieij=3\sum_{j} tie_{ij} = 3 ) = 0.5, probability an agent with outdegree = 3 will create a tie (v. maintain a tie).
  3. Transition_Probability(change = creation| ∑jtieij=4\sum_{j} tie_{ij} = 4 ) = 0.4, probability an agent with outdegree = 4 will create a tie (v. maintain a tie).

2. Generate a directed random baseline network:

  1. For each agent:

  2. Assign a random outdegree value, �, with the following probability (values in this probability distribution are taken from CILS4EU):

  1. P(� = 0) = 0.048, probability of having no ties at baseline.

  2. P(� = 1) = 0.080, probability of having 1 tie at baseline.

  3. P(� = 2) = 0.164, probability of having 2 ties at baseline.

  4. P(� = 3) = 0.228, probability of having 3 ties at baseline.

  5. P(� = 4) = 0.261, probability of having 4 ties at baseline.

  6. P(� = 5) = 0.219, probability of having 5 ties at baseline.

  1. Create � ties with randomly selected alters.

  1. For each agent: assign a binary depression indicator value, Dego,D _ { e g o } , with probability of success pdepression=0.2p _ { d e p r e s s i o n } = \ 0 . 2 . That is, on average, 20% of agents are ‘depressed.

  2. For depressed agents: set ������������ (i.e., the probability of tie creation for depressed agents) and ��������������� (i.e., the probability of tie maintenance for depressed agents). Factorial Experiment for Assessing SAOM Estimated Coefficients. To assess the ability of the standard SAOM to uncover the true data generating process instantiated in the ABM algorithm described above, we utilize a factorial experimental design with distinct tie creation and maintenance probabilities for depressed and non-depressed agents. For full replicability, here we estimated standard SAOMs with RSiena version 1.4.7 and estimation algorithm parameters: seed = 9999, ΠΠ𝐮̂=1000(i.e.\boldsymbol { \mathrm { \Pi } } \boldsymbol { \mathrm { \Pi } } \boldsymbol { \mathrm { \hat { \mathbf { u } } } } = 1 0 0 0 \left( \mathrm { i . e . } \right. ., the number of iterations in phase 3), nsub = 4 (i.e., the number of subphases in phase 2), and maximum outdegree set to 5 for the microsteps.

Table D.1 presents key information for the factorial experiment. The table should be read from the perspective of depressed agents. That is, a negative (positive) ‘creation probability difference’ means that, when compared to non-depressed agents, depressed agents are less

(more) likely to create ties. Similarly, a negative (positive) ‘maintenance probability difference means that, when compared to non-depressed agents, depressed agents are less (more) likely to maintain their ties. Since our design is grounded on depression-based creation and maintenance ‘probability differences,’ there are 81 unique combinations or conditions based on the 9 unique creation probability differences and 9 unique maintenance probability differences listed in Table D.1. We ran each of the 81 conditions 100 times, estimating a standard SAOM for each of them. Here we analyze the resulting depression ego coefficients from said SAOMs.

Agent-Based Model Simulation Results. For ease of exposition, we limit our discussion of the results to: (a) the mean value of the estimated depression ego effect in each of the 81 conditions of the experiment; and (b) the proportion of positive depression ego effects in each of the 81 conditions of the experiment. As detailed in Figures D.1 and D.2 below, when both the creation and maintenance probabilities go in the same direction, the standard SAOM always captures the data-generating process accurately. For instance, as shown in the lower left quadrant of Figures D.1 and D.2, when depressed agents are less likely to both maintain ties and create

ties vis-à-vis non-depressed agents (i.e., maintenance probability difference ranges -0.8 to -0.2 and creation probability difference ranges -0.8 to -0.2), all standard SAOMs correctly estimate negative depression effects (i.e., all proportions in the lower-left quadrant of Figure D.2 are 0 indicating that all estimated effects were negative). Given that both our systematic review and meta-analysis of the standard SAOM literature shows that published studies do not exhibit consistently negative depression ego effects (see Figure 3) and that our own standard SAOM results also do not exhibit a consistently negative depression ego effect (see Tables 3, 4, and 5), our ABM results suggest that the empirical maintenance and creation depression ego effects might not be both negative.

Accurate results are also observed when both tie creation and maintenance are positively associated with depression (D), that is, across all estimated SAOMs a positive coefficient is observed in the upper-right quadrant in Figure D.2 (i.e., maintenance probability difference ranges 0.2 to 0.8 and creation probability difference ranges 0.2 to 0.8). Given that both our systematic review and meta-analysis of the standard SAOM literature shows that published studies do not exhibit consistently positive depression ego effects (see Figure 3) and that our own standard SAOM results also do not exhibit a consistently positive depression ego effect (see Tables 3, 4, and 5), our ABM results suggest that the empirical maintenance and creation depression ego effects might not be both positive.

Finally, when D truly does not have an impact on tie maintenance and creation (creation probability difference = maintenance probability difference = 0), on average, 56% of the estimated standard SAOM coefficients are positive and are comparatively small in size, with an average value of -0.001. This suggests standard SAOMs do an accurate representation of this particular scenario, which represents the absence of a depression-sociality link.

Critically, however, when tie creation and tie maintenance go in opposite directions (i.e., on the main diagonal and on the upper left and lower right quadrant in Figures D.1 and D.2), the standard SAOM is not reliable. For example, we note that coefficients exhibit different results across simulations under scenarios where creation and maintenance have the same strength but go in opposite directions:

A. 0.2 maintenance probability difference and -0.2 creation probability difference: 45% of estimated coefficients are positive.

B. -0.2 maintenance probability difference and 0.2 creation probability difference: 54% of estimated coefficients are positive

C. 0.4 maintenance probability difference and -0.4 creation probability difference: 64% of estimated coefficients are positive.

D. -0.4 maintenance probability difference and 0.4 creation probability difference: 31% of estimated coefficients are positive.

E. 0.6 maintenance probability difference and -0.6 creation probability difference: 72% of estimated coefficients are positive.

F. -0.6 maintenance probability difference and 0.6 creation probability difference: 26% of estimated coefficients are positive.

In these scenarios, there is great variability in the sign of the parameter estimate, with negative and positive values being likely outcomes.

In sum, our simulations suggest that unless depression-based tie maintenance and creation go in the same direction (which is, ultimately, an empirical question), the standard SAOM might produce unreliable results, including unreliable null results. This supports the idea that in SAOMs “if effect X is included as the [‘standard’] evaluation effect, the implicit assumption that underlies this modeling decision is that the parameters for [X’s effect on] creation and maintenance are identical (and identical to the evaluation parameter).” (Block 2014: 107-108). Critically, our non-standard SAOMs empirical results (see Tables 6 and 7) suggest that depression-based tie maintenance and tie creation go in different directions, that is, they might not be identical.
